body.estimand_functional: \(\rho_n^*\asymp r_{\mathrm{mix}}(n)\asymp r_{\mathrm{test}}(n)\), conditional on proving the two independent optimizations match in oeq:complete-frontier

sampling_model.units: \(O_1,\ldots,O_n\) are independent and identically distributed observed margins of a law in \(\mathcal P(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L,d)\).
sampling_model.treatment: Binary \(A\) has unknown propensity \(e\) under the observational experiment; the comparison experiment supplies the exact function \(e_P\) to the test.
sampling_model.outcome: Observed and potential outcomes are binary. The pointwise restrictions \(m_0,m_1\in[1/4,3/4]\) apply to the canonical continuous representatives of the two conditional-mean equivalence classes.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: No nuisance estimator and no nuisance convergence rate is part of the class; all tuning is a deterministic function of \(n,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,d,L\).

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Theorem 1 gives the pointwise CATE-estimation minimax rate with a nuisance-smoothness elbow, and Theorem 2 gives attainability under additional design-density conditions.
Theorems 4 and 6 give fixed-alternative consistency and a local weak limit for quantitative homogeneity tests over structured rule classes under the paper's nuisance conditions.

Theorems 1--2 establish asymptotic normality for propensity-reweighted pairwise and multisample adjusted \(U\)-statistics under consistent propensity estimation, independent stratum samples, stable positive sample fractions, and pointwise overlap.

Section 3 derives joint asymptotic normality and Gaussian-simulation calibration for multisample \(U\)-statistics testing equality of additive treatment effects across a fixed collection of mutually independent prespecified strata.

Theorem 6 gives asymptotic level, fixed-alternative consistency, and nontrivial \(n^{-1/2}\)-local power for a multiplier-bootstrap test of homogeneous restricted CATE with possibly right-censored duration outcomes.

Section 4 gives a conservative finite-sample-valid Fisher randomization test for the sharp null of one unknown constant individual treatment effect by maximizing randomization \(p\)-values over a confidence set for that nuisance effect.

The main martingale-transformation results give asymptotic level for a permutation test of a constant marginal-distribution shift with an estimated nuisance shift, retaining exact level only for the more restrictive sharp null.
Theorems 3 and 7 give asymptotic chi-square tests of equality of finitely many score-defined group average treatment effects under complete randomization, with sample splitting or cross-fitting.
Theorems 4.1 and 5.2 give matching nonasymptotic binned conditional-independence critical radii for fixed discrete responses and a continuous conditioning variable under total-variation smoothness.
Theorems 6 and 7 give null validity and spline minimax power for projected conditional covariance under common smoothness and nondegeneracy restrictions.
Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 characterize bias, variance, and optimal separate wavelet resolutions for estimating a signed expected conditional covariance functional.
The main minimax theorems derive sharp heteroskedasticity-detection rates using a squared first-difference proxy under a rough unknown mean.
Theorem 1 gives asymptotic normality and type-I error control for an intra-fold split CATE-variance statistic under explicit nuisance learner-rate conditions.
The paper proves that the propensity score is ancillary for semiparametrically efficient estimation of the regular average treatment effect under ignorability.
Theorems 3.3 and 3.4 give asymptotic null validity and consistency against smooth local sieve alternatives for the null that the conditional average treatment effect is constant.

The paper develops \(L_1\)-type tests based on uniformly consistent nonparametric kernel estimators for conditional treatment-effect restrictions and proves asymptotically correct size, fixed-alternative consistency, and power against some local alternatives.
Section 1 records the classical nonadaptive Hölder goodness-of-fit boundary, and the paper establishes the iterated-logarithmic price of adaptation in wavelet testing.

body.tldr: The paper determines the fixed-sample minimax scale at which observational data can detect any nonconstant binary-outcome CATE when the propensity, baseline regression, and CATE have separate rough Hölder indices. The known-propensity experiment reduces by a bounded pseudo-outcome to the classical Spokoiny Hölder goodness-of-fit benchmark, while an explicit profiled fourth-order statistic gives a uniformly calibrated all-regime observational upper envelope and already matches that benchmark in a broad asymmetric region. The unresolved kernel is represented by two independent finite optimizations: \(r_{\mathrm{test}}\) minimizes a fully displayed multiresolution bias and four-projection stochastic envelope, whereas \(r_{\mathrm{mix}}\) maximizes explicit CATE separation over finite bounded atomic laws subject to a displayed algebraic likelihood-divergence envelope. The common sharp rate is named only if an attaining test and same-class constant-CATE null mixture prove these optimizations equivalent. The final experiment frontier states exactly when revealing the propensity changes detection, without smoothness adaptation, forest certification, or interpreting non-rejection as homogeneity.

project_justification.gap: Published CATE-homogeneity procedures establish asymptotic validity or power under structured directions and nuisance learner conditions; published minimax results instead treat pointwise CATE estimation, conditional independence under different geometry, signed expected covariance, or heteroskedasticity. None gives the fixed-sample critical radius over the identical binary causal class with three separate Hölder indices and an unknown constant null.
project_justification.niche: The missing object is the rough-confounding testing modulus itself, including sparse occupancy, asymmetric propensity and baseline smoothness, boundary logarithms, and the statistical value of revealing the true propensity.
project_justification.fill: The analysis starts from an exact binned covariance identity, profiles the unknown constant inside a fourth-order statistic, exposes every bias and complete-Hoeffding calibration term in a finite testing optimization, and pairs it with a separate finite mixture optimization over explicit bounded atomic amplitude laws whose second moment exactly matches the displayed rough-case repeated-observation coefficient. A common sharp rate is reported only after these objects are attained and matched.

body.related_work: The direct-comparator census treats a source as direct when its formal null requires equality or constancy of mean, unit-level, subgroup, or distributional treatment effects; zero-effect restrictions and testing-method donors are retained separately. \begin{center}\scriptsize\begin{tabular}{p{0.09\linewidth}p{0.20\linewidth}p{0.18\linewidth}p{0.20\linewidth}p{0.19\linewidth}}\textbf{Source} & \textbf{Model class} & \textbf{Null} & \textbf{Separation or alternative} & \textbf{Finite-sample guarantee}\\ \hline KBRW (2024) & Binary-treatment causal Hölder model & No testing null & Pointwise CATE estimation loss & No testing guarantee.\\ Crump et al. (2008) & Unconfounded treatment with growing series regressions & \(\tau(x)=c\) & Smooth sieve departures & Asymptotic size and consistency only.\\ Sant'Anna (2021) & Iid right-censored durations under unconfoundedness, with a binary-IV extension & Restricted CATE is constant almost surely & Fixed and \(n^{-1/2}\)-local integrated-moment alternatives & Theorem 6 is asymptotic; multiplier-bootstrap calibration is not uniform finite-sample.\\ Dai--Stern (2022) & Mutually independent treatment and control samples in finitely many prespecified strata & Additive treatment effects are equal across strata & Pairwise multisample \(U\)-functionals & Section 3 uses joint asymptotic normality and Gaussian simulation, not finite-sample uniform calibration.\\ Dai--Shen--Stern (2023) & Independent observational strata reweighted by estimated propensities & Average treatment effects are equal across strata & Adjusted multisample \(U\)-functionals & Theorems 1--2 give asymptotic normality under consistent propensity estimation and stable stratum fractions.\\ Ding--Feller--Miratrix (2016) & Fixed potential outcomes under a known randomized assignment & One unknown constant individual treatment effect, or a specified finite-dimensional effect model & Distributional test statistics under Fisher randomization & The confidence-set maximized test is finite-sample valid but targets a sharp unit-level null.\\ Chung--Olivares (2021) & Two randomized samples from marginal outcome distributions & The treated distribution is an unknown constant shift of the control distribution & Supremum distance after martingale transformation & General validity is asymptotic; exactness is retained only for the sharper known-shift null.\\ Imai--Li (2025) & Iid units with complete randomization and an external or split-sample score & A fixed number of score-defined group average effects are equal & Finite-dimensional GATE contrasts & Theorems 3 and 7 give asymptotic chi-square calibration, not an omnibus continuous-CATE guarantee.\\ Dukes et al. (2026) & Observational causal model with a structured rule class and estimated nuisances & Quantitative CATE homogeneity over that rule class & Structured policy-direction contrasts & Theorems 2, 4, and 6 give asymptotic size, fixed power, and local weak limits.\\ Yu (2026) & Observational causal model with learner-rate and nondegeneracy conditions & \(\operatorname{Var}\{\tau(X)\}=0\) & Fixed positive CATE variance & Theorem 1 is asymptotic and assumes nuisance rates.\\ Chang et al. (2015) & Unconfounded treatment with kernel conditional-mean estimators & Zero, nonpositive, or distributional conditional-effect restrictions & \(L_1\)-type fixed and local alternatives & Asymptotically correct size and consistency only.\\ NBW (2021) & Discrete responses and a continuous conditioner with conditional-law smoothness & Conditional independence & Total-variation distance to the null class & Theorems 4.1 and 5.2 give nonasymptotic minimax bounds in a different model.\\ PCM (2024) & Conditional-mean model with spline regressions and common smoothness & Conditional mean independence & Squared projected conditional mean & Theorems 6--7 give uniform asymptotic, not finite-sample, guarantees. \end{tabular}\end{center} SantAnna2021, Section 4.2 and Theorem 6, is the closest continuous-covariate extension of the Crump constant-CATE null, but its censored-duration integrated moments and root-\(n\) directional alternatives do not define a three-index Hölder minimax radius. DaiStern2022, Section 3, and DaiShenStern2023, Theorems 1--2, compare average effects across a fixed finite stratum geometry; neither tests arbitrary variation over the full-support cube nor provides uniform finite-sample calibration. DingFellerMiratrix2016 supplies exact-design validity for a sharper unit-level constant-effect null, ChungOlivares2021 supplies asymptotic distribution-shift permutation validity, and ImaiLi2025 tests equality of finitely many score-defined GATEs; these nulls can respectively be stronger than, different from, or coarser than continuous CATE constancy. CrumpHotzImbensMitnik2008 remains the closest uncensored unknown-constant-CATE predecessor, but its series asymptotics do not furnish the present fixed-sample radius. ChangLeeWhang2015 and DukesStensrudBrioschiHudson2026 establish asymptotic conditional-effect tests under kernel or structured-rule formulations. Yu2026VarianceHTE studies the same variance-zero characterization under supplied learner rates. KennedyBalakrishnanRobinsWasserman2024 concerns pointwise CATE estimation; its loss and support-modified lower construction do not solve global homogeneity testing. NeykovBalakrishnanWasserman2021 and LundborgKimShahSamworth2024 supply testing machinery under different null manifolds and metrics. McGrathMukherjee2026 informs separate nuisance resolutions for a signed covariance functional, and KotekalKundu2025 informs rough-regression proxy design under a Gaussian likelihood. Spokoiny1996 supplies only the known-propensity goodness-of-fit benchmark, and Hahn1998 supplies only the regular ATE ancillarity comparator.
body.technical_internal_limitation: At \(d=\gamma=1\) and \(\alpha=\beta=1/10\), def:rough-prior-diagnostic is a fully legal localized family: every null component has \(\tau\equiv1/8\), and its sign mixture matches a heterogeneous alternative for one observation. The first failure is the two-observation treatment moment \(q_{\ell}^2\sum_j b_{j,\ell}(x)b_{j,\ell}(z)\) created when observations share a latent local sign. The chosen \(q_{\ell}=\epsilon_{\mathrm{diag}}\ell^{1/2}\) also keeps the induced alternative CATE Lipschitz, so the diagnostic does not attain the larger rough-nuisance amplitude \(\ell^{1/5}\). The feasible set \(\Theta_n\) replaces free moment coordinates by one finite atomic law \(\nu_\theta\): its exact second moment makes the displayed binary two-observation coefficient zero, while its third and fourth moments and support radius determine all remaining terms in \(V_n\). The single-resolution sparse-bin rate is only an upper envelope and may be an artifact of third- and fourth-order Hoeffding projections.
body.honest_scope: The known-propensity rate is a standard Spokoiny-type benchmark transported by a bounded pseudo-outcome and carries no novelty claim. The objects \(r_{\mathrm{mix}}\) and \(r_{\mathrm{test}}\) are independently evaluable finite optimizations, not definitions through \(\rho_n^*\); proving that their envelopes are attained and that their orders match, simplifying the resulting regimes and transition logarithms, and deriving the converse direction of the propensity equality frontier remain open. The single-resolution envelope and no-penalty region remain theorem targets. Smoothness adaptation, unknown covariate density, outcomes outside \(\{0,1\}\), local overlap, and validation of any existing forest are outside scope. Under known propensity the result must reduce to \(n^{-2\gamma/(4\gamma+d)}\); when \(\alpha+\beta\ge\gamma\) and \(d\le4\gamma\), the observational result must reduce to the same rate.
